lines: Picture one real, running system that answers absolutely everything through a single worker, with no second worker ever touching the actual work at the same time.
By every intuition about getting more done, that should be slow.
And yet this particular one, watched directly, handles an enormous stream of requests a second without breaking a sweat.
Worth reasoning through before the explanation lands.
Is that speed happening in spite of having only one worker, the way something manages to be fast despite an obvious handicap?
Or is the single worker itself the actual source of the speed, not a limitation it's working around at all?
answer: It's the second one — the single worker is the reason, not the obstacle.
Splitting work across many workers always costs something: time spent coordinating who touches what, and waiting for others to get out of the way.
A single worker never pays either of those costs, and that saved cost turns out to be larger than whatever parallel work was given up to get it.

lines: Here's exactly where that one worker's job ends and starts.
Every actual piece of work always lands on that same single worker, with no exceptions.
A handful of extra helpers do exist, but only to move bytes to and from the network — never to do the work itself — and they're switched off unless someone deliberately turns them on.
Now, how this system avoids losing everything the moment power is cut.
One approach takes a full copy of everything at set intervals, which means anything that happened since the last copy is gone if the system stops uncleanly.
A second approach instead writes down every single change as it happens, so replaying that record rebuilds exactly what was there, with nothing missing in between.
Here's a risk that sounds abstract until it's measured directly.
A second, standing copy of this system doesn't apply every change the instant the first one does — it's told about changes after the fact, on its own schedule.

Watched for real right after a burst of changes: the original already calls those changes done, and the standing copy is measurably still behind — so if the original died at that exact instant, work already called done would simply be gone.
One specific way of spreading this system across many machines, worth naming on its own.
Every possible piece of data it could ever hold is mapped into one fixed set of buckets, decided once and never changing size.
Each of those buckets belongs to exactly one machine at a time, which is what makes it possible to know, for any piece of data, exactly which machine is responsible for it.
One last piece, and it has nothing to do with how any of this works technically.
This system started out under one of the most permissive kinds of open licensing there is, until its maker switched to terms that restrict how competitors can resell it.

That switch is exactly why a close, independently governed copy of the old version exists today under the original permissive terms — and why the maker later added yet another licensing option on top of its new ones.
Pulling the whole topic back together.
A single worker is the actual source of the speed, not a cost paid for it.
Writing down every change avoids the gap a periodic full copy leaves open. A standing copy told about changes after the fact can genuinely be caught behind, measured directly.
Spreading data across fixed, owned buckets is how this system scales past one machine at all. And which of these systems to even run is now, in part, a licensing decision.
One closing scenario, worth reasoning through before the explanation lands.
A team needs a setup where nothing already called done can ever be lost, not even if the machine crashes outright.
Of this topic's own default choices, which one would they have to change, and to what?
answer: Not the periodic-full-copy approach — that one accepts losing a little by design, no matter how it's tuned.
They'd switch to the write-down-every-change approach, and set it to force each change to durable storage aggressively rather than on a relaxed schedule.
That's strictly slower than trusting the periodic copy alone, which is exactly the trade a team makes once losing anything at all stops being acceptable.
